title: Climate finance

definition.text: Money, such as loans, grants or government budget spending, used to cut greenhouse gas emissions, adapt to climate change or build resilience.

facts.text: The money can come from private or public sources and can pass through intermediaries such as multilateral development banks and development agencies.
Under the UN Climate Convention, climate finance means transfers of public money from high-income to low- and middle-income countries, in line with their duty to provide new and additional resources.
It has two main subcategories: mitigation finance, which aims to reduce emissions, and adaptation finance, which responds to the consequences of climate change.
Global climate finance was estimated at around $1.3 trillion per year in 2021/2022, up from more than US$600 billion in 2019 by one estimate.
Most of it, 84% in 2021/2022, is raised and spent within the same country.
A 2024 report estimated that flows must rise at least sixfold on 2021/2022 levels, to $8.5 trillion per year by 2030.
Public budgets are widely seen as too small to meet the need, so private finance is expected to be important for closing the gap.
Its main challenges are measuring and tracking flows, fair support for developing countries, and giving private investors suitable incentives.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
related: New Collective Quantified Goal on climate finance

definition.text: Investment that aims to reduce global greenhouse gas emissions.

facts.text: Mitigation accounts for over 90% of worldwide investment in climate finance.
Around 70% of mitigation money has gone to renewable energy; energy efficiency and transport are the other key sectors.
Of the estimated US$83.3 billion provided to developing countries in 2020, US$48.6 billion, or 58%, targeted mitigation.
The IEA estimates that keeping warming below 2 Celsius needs an average of $3.5 trillion a year of energy-sector investment until 2050.
The 2018 Biennial Assessment put mitigation financing needs for 2020 to 2030 at US$1.7-2.4 trillion per year.

definition.text: Climate finance that pays for responding to the consequences of climate change.

facts.text: It comes from governments, development finance institutions and multilateral climate funds, and from private sources such as banks, investors, companies and households.
Around 98% of tracked adaptation finance has come from public sources, partly because adaptation projects rarely have a clear income stream or attractive return.
Only around 4-8% of total climate finance has gone to adaptation.
Benefits can be large: every US$1 billion invested against coastal flooding is estimated to cut economic damages by US$14 billion.
A 2023 study put adaptation costs for all developing countries at around US$215 billion per year up to 2030.
Of adaptation-specific funding, 63% came as loans and 36% as grants, and only 66% of committed amounts were paid out.

title: Adaptation finance gap
article: Climate finance#Current levels of financing and the finance gap

definition.text: The difference between the estimated cost of adapting to climate change and the money available for adaptation.

facts.text: International public finance to developing countries for adaptation stayed well below US$30 billion per year between 2017 and 2021.
On 2017–2021 data, estimated needs are around 10-18 times current public flows, and the gap has widened since earlier assessments.
A 2023 study of 85 countries' plans estimated developing countries' adaptation needs at US$387 billion a year up to 2030.
More public and private finance, remittances and reform of how vulnerable countries' debts are managed could help close it.

definition.text: The shortfall between the climate investment that is needed and what is actually provided.

facts.text: Estimates of the gap vary with the places, sectors, timescale, target and assumptions used.
Research finds bilateral climate finance well below official figures, partly because there is no agreed definition of international climate finance and no oversight.
This has let non-climate projects be counted and raised doubts about official reporting.

definition.text: Funds governed by several national governments together that pay out money for climate action.

facts.text: As of 2022, the UNFCCC coordinated five: the Green Climate Fund, the Adaptation Fund, the Least Developed Countries Fund, the Special Climate Change Fund and the Global Environment Facility.
The World Bank coordinates the Climate Investment Funds, active since 2008, made up of the Clean Technology Fund and the Strategic Climate Fund.
Some give only grants; others also use concessional loans, equity and risk tools meant to crowd in other finance.
In 2016 the four main multilateral climate funds approved $2.78 billion of project support.

definition.text: Climate investment from private sources such as banks, pension funds, insurers, asset managers, companies and households.

facts.text: Public budgets are often too small for large infrastructure projects, especially in lower-income countries, so private money is seen as needed to cover the shortfall.
Climate-friendly projects can cost more up front and carry more risk than fossil-fuel ones, so they must be bankable to attract private investors.
Over 90% of private climate flows are estimated to stay within national borders.
The IMF and OECD warn that private capital alone cannot close the gap, since many adaptation and innovation projects bring high social benefits but low private returns.

definition.text: A deal in which a country's debt is repaid on new discounted terms and the repayments, in local currency, are redirected to domestic climate projects.

facts.text: Projects funded this way can include carbon sequestration, renewable energy and conservation of biodiversity and oceans.
In one Argentine swap, $38,100,000 of debt was addressed and $3,100,000 went to biodiversity, forest and other climate work.
Seychelles redirected $27 million of debt to marine parks, ocean conservation and ecotourism in a similar debt-for-nature swap.

definition.text: Finance that reduces the carbon footprint of ocean-related economic activity and benefits the marine environment.

facts.text: It is part of sustainable finance and overlaps with climate finance, funding offshore wind, zero-emission shipping and the restoration of mangroves and seagrass.
The World Economic Forum says US$175 billion a year is needed to reach SDG 14, the most underfunded of the 17 SDGs.
Its tools include blue bonds, the marine counterpart of green bonds.

title: Green Climate Fund

definition.text: A climate finance fund set up under the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change to help developing countries with mitigation and adaptation.

facts.text: It is considered the world's largest fund of its kind and is the largest of the five multilateral climate funds coordinated by the UNFCCC.
It was named in the 2009 Copenhagen Accord, formally established at the 2010 Cancun conference, and its governing instrument was adopted in Durban in 2011.
It is based in Songdo, South Korea, and governed by a 24-member board with a secretariat.
As of November 2026 its portfolio was over $22.3 billion USD, or over $87.1 billion USD including co-financing.

One of its most controversial features is the Private Sector Facility: many rich countries want it to attract institutional investors, while developing countries and NGOs want pro-poor finance for small firms.
In March 2015 its board refused an explicit ban on fossil fuel projects, effectively allowing coal plants to be funded.

prerequisites: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change
contested_note: Rich and developing countries disagree over whether its private-sector arm should court large investors or support small firms, and over relying on private rather than pledged public money.

definition.text: The rule that climate finance given to developing countries should be new money, additional to existing development aid.

facts.text: The Cancun agreements require such finance, including through the Green Climate Fund, to be new and additional.
New means pledges should come on top of those made in earlier years.
There is no strict definition of additionality, which has already caused problems, and even fraud, in judging CDM emission reductions.
